topics.title: DSA Scope
topics.description: Understand the scope of Data Structures and Algorithms, the problems they help solve, the major areas covered in DSA, and how these concepts are applied in software development and technical interviews.

sections.title: What is the scope of DSA?
sections.content:
Data Structures and Algorithms (DSA) covers the techniques used to organize data and solve computational problems efficiently. Data structures determine how information is stored and accessed, while algorithms define the steps used to process that information and produce a result.

The scope of DSA extends from basic structures such as arrays, strings, linked lists, stacks, and queues to more advanced structures such as trees, graphs, heaps, hash tables, and specialized data structures. It also includes algorithms for searching, sorting, traversal, recursion, dynamic programming, greedy problem solving, and graph processing.

Learning DSA is not limited to solving interview questions. These concepts are useful when designing software that needs efficient data access, processing, memory usage, and scalability.

sections.title: Data structures covered in DSA
sections.content:
A major part of DSA focuses on choosing an appropriate data structure for a particular problem. Common linear data structures include arrays, strings, linked lists, stacks, and queues. These structures store elements in sequences but provide different ways of accessing and modifying data.

Non-linear data structures include trees and graphs, which represent hierarchical or interconnected relationships. Heaps are commonly used when applications need efficient access to the minimum or maximum element, while hash tables provide fast average-case lookup using keys.

The goal is not simply to memorize different data structures. Developers should understand how each structure works, its time and space requirements, and the situations in which it is appropriate.

sections.title: Algorithms covered in DSA
sections.content:
Algorithms form another major part of DSA. They provide systematic procedures for solving problems and processing data. Common topics include searching algorithms, sorting algorithms, recursion, divide-and-conquer techniques, greedy algorithms, backtracking, dynamic programming, and graph algorithms.

For example, searching algorithms determine how efficiently a required value can be located, while sorting algorithms arrange data according to a defined order. Graph algorithms can be used to explore relationships between connected objects, find paths, or determine properties of a network.

Many algorithms can solve the same problem in different ways. Comparing their time and space complexity helps developers choose an approach that remains practical as the input size increases.

sections.title: Complexity analysis
sections.content:
Understanding the efficiency of an algorithm is an important part of the scope of DSA. Complexity analysis describes how the resource requirements of an algorithm change as the size of the input grows.

Time complexity measures how the running time grows with input size, while space complexity describes the additional memory required by an algorithm. Big O notation is commonly used to express an upper-bound growth rate, with examples such as O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), and O(n²).

Complexity analysis allows developers to compare different approaches without depending only on the execution time observed on one particular machine or dataset.

sections.title: DSA in software development
sections.content:
DSA concepts appear in many areas of software development. Efficient data structures can improve database-related processing, caching, search operations, scheduling, memory management, networking, and application logic. Algorithms are also used internally by many libraries and frameworks to perform operations efficiently.

For example, a hash-based structure can provide efficient key-based lookups, a priority queue can help process tasks according to priority, and graph algorithms can be used to model connections between systems or entities.

The practical value of DSA comes from recognizing the underlying problem and selecting a suitable combination of data structure and algorithm rather than applying a particular technique simply because it is familiar.

sections.title: DSA for technical interviews
sections.content:
DSA is commonly included in technical interviews because it provides a structured way to evaluate problem-solving and programming skills. Interview problems may require candidates to select a suitable data structure, develop an algorithm, analyze its complexity, and explain the trade-offs involved.

Typical interview topics include arrays, strings, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs, sorting, searching, recursion, backtracking, greedy algorithms, and dynamic programming.

Preparing for DSA interviews is more effective when the focus is placed on understanding patterns and reasoning. A strong preparation process usually involves learning the underlying concept, solving problems of increasing difficulty, analyzing alternative solutions, and reviewing the complexity of each approach.

sections.title: How to approach learning DSA
sections.content:
DSA is easier to learn when concepts are studied progressively. A typical learning path starts with complexity analysis and basic data structures before moving to searching, sorting, recursion, trees, heaps, graphs, and more advanced problem-solving techniques.

Each topic should be understood from both an implementation and problem-solving perspective. For example, after learning a stack, it is useful to understand its operations, complexity, implementation, and common applications before solving problems that depend on stack behavior.

As the concepts become familiar, practice should focus on identifying patterns, selecting appropriate data structures, writing efficient algorithms, handling edge cases, and explaining why the chosen solution works.

topics.title: Assumed Knowledge
topics.description: Understand the foundational programming concepts and problem-solving skills that are useful before starting a structured Data Structures and Algorithms course.

sections.title: Programming fundamentals
sections.content:
Before learning Data Structures and Algorithms, it is useful to have a basic understanding of programming. You should be comfortable with variables, data types, operators, conditional statements, loops, and functions or methods.

You should also understand how a program executes instructions and how values are passed between different parts of a program. These fundamentals make it easier to focus on the data structure or algorithm being studied rather than struggling with basic programming syntax.

sections.title: Arrays and basic data handling
sections.content:
A basic understanding of arrays is helpful because arrays are one of the most frequently used structures in DSA. You should know how to create an array, access elements using indexes, update values, iterate through elements, and determine the length of an array.

You should also be comfortable working with collections of values and performing simple operations such as finding an element, calculating a sum, counting occurrences, or identifying a maximum or minimum value.

sections.title: Functions, recursion, and problem decomposition
sections.content:
DSA problems are often easier to solve when a larger problem is divided into smaller, well-defined steps. A basic understanding of functions or methods helps you organize these steps and reuse logic.

Some DSA topics also use recursion, where a function solves a problem by calling itself with a smaller version of the same problem. You do not need advanced recursion knowledge before starting, but you should understand function calls, parameters, return values, and the idea of a base condition.

sections.title: Basic object-oriented concepts
sections.content:
A detailed understanding of object-oriented programming is not required for learning the core ideas of DSA, but basic knowledge of classes, objects, fields, and methods can be useful when implementing custom data structures.

For example, linked lists, trees, graphs, and other structures are often implemented using classes or node objects. Understanding how objects store data and reference other objects makes these implementations easier to follow.

sections.title: Basic mathematics
sections.content:
DSA does not require advanced mathematics, but some basic mathematical reasoning is useful. You should be comfortable with numbers, comparisons, arithmetic operations, powers, logarithms at a conceptual level, and simple mathematical patterns.

These concepts become useful when analyzing algorithm complexity. For example, understanding how repeatedly dividing a problem by two leads to logarithmic growth helps when studying algorithms such as binary search.

sections.title: Basic problem-solving skills
sections.content:
DSA is primarily about learning how to approach problems systematically. You should be comfortable reading a problem statement, identifying the input and expected output, breaking the problem into smaller parts, and thinking through possible edge cases.

It is not necessary to know advanced algorithms before starting the course. The important prerequisite is a willingness to reason about different approaches and understand why one solution may require fewer operations or less memory than another.

sections.title: Programming language familiarity
sections.content:
DSA concepts can be learned using many programming languages, including Java, Python, C++, JavaScript, and others. You should choose a language whose basic syntax you already understand.

The course should focus on the underlying data structures and algorithms rather than language-specific features. Once the algorithm is understood, the same idea can generally be implemented in another programming language with appropriate syntax changes.

sections.title: What you do not need to know beforehand
sections.content:
You do not need to have prior knowledge of advanced data structures, complex algorithms, dynamic programming, graph theory, or competitive programming before starting a DSA course. These topics can be introduced progressively as part of the learning path.

You also do not need to memorize implementations before learning the concepts. Understanding how a structure works, what operations it supports, and the complexity of those operations is more important than memorizing code.

topics.shortDescription: Learn the programming, mathematical, and problem-solving fundamentals that are useful before starting Data Structures and Algorithms.

topics.title: Big-O Notation
topics.description: Understand Big-O notation, how algorithm performance changes as input size grows, and how time and space complexity are used to evaluate and compare data structures and algorithms.

sections.title: What is Big-O notation?
sections.content:
Big-O notation is a mathematical notation used to describe how the resource requirements of an algorithm grow as the size of its input increases. It is most commonly used to analyze time complexity and space complexity.

Time complexity describes how the amount of computation grows with the input size, while space complexity describes how additional memory requirements grow.

Big-O focuses on the growth rate rather than the exact execution time. For example, an algorithm that performs 5n operations and another that performs 100n operations are both O(n), because both grow linearly as n increases.

Big-O is useful because it allows different algorithms to be compared without depending entirely on a particular machine, processor speed, or programming language implementation.

sections.title: Understanding input size
Constant time - O(1)
sections.content:
An operation has O(1), or constant time, complexity when the amount of work does not grow with the size of the input.

For example, accessing an array element using a known index is generally a constant-time operation:

```java
int value = numbers[5];
```

Whether the array contains 10 elements or 10 million elements, accessing the element at index 5 requires a similar amount of work.

O(1) does not necessarily mean that the operation takes exactly one machine instruction. It means that the growth of the operation count is independent of n.

sections.title: Linear time - O(n)
Logarithmic time - O(log n)
Quadratic time - O(n²)
Cubic time - O(n³)
O(n log n) complexity
Exponential time - O(2ⁿ)
Dropping constants
Dropping lower-order terms
Time complexity
Space complexity
Best-case, average-case, and worst-case complexity
Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta
sections.content:
Big-O, Big-Omega, and Big-Theta are related asymptotic notations used to describe algorithm growth.

Big-O is commonly used to describe an upper bound on growth. Big-Omega describes a lower bound, while Big-Theta describes a tight asymptotic bound when both upper and lower bounds match.

For example, a function that grows linearly can be described as Θ(n) when its growth is tightly bounded by linear functions.

In practical DSA discussions and technical interviews, Big-O notation is used very frequently when describing worst-case complexity, but understanding the distinction between these notations provides a more complete understanding of asymptotic analysis.

sections.title: Comparing common complexities
sections.content:
Different complexity classes grow at very different rates as the input becomes larger. Common complexity classes include O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(n³), and O(2ⁿ).

A simplified progression from slower growth to faster growth is:

```text
O(1)
O(log n)
O(n)
O(n log n)
O(n²)
O(n³)
O(2ⁿ)
```

This ordering helps build intuition about scalability. However, the complexity class alone does not determine practical performance in every situation. Constants, input constraints, memory usage, implementation details, and the actual operations being performed can also matter.

topics.title: Imperative Programming
topics.description: Understand the imperative programming paradigm, how programs execute through explicit instructions and state changes, and how variables, conditions, loops, functions, and mutable data are used when implementing data structures and algorithms.

sections.title: What is imperative programming?
sections.content:
Imperative programming is a programming paradigm in which a program describes the steps required to perform a task. The program executes a sequence of instructions that can create, read, and modify data as execution progresses.

The word imperative refers to giving the computer explicit instructions about what to do. A typical imperative program uses variables, assignments, conditional statements, loops, and functions to control execution.

Languages such as Java, C, C++, Python, and JavaScript support imperative programming constructs. These concepts are especially important in DSA because many algorithms are expressed as a sequence of operations performed on data.

Why imperative programming matters in DSA
sections.content:
A strong understanding of imperative programming makes it easier to implement and reason about DSA solutions. Most introductory DSA problems require direct control over variables, loops, conditions, indexes, references, and data structure state.

When solving a DSA problem, the solution can first be expressed as a sequence of logical steps and then translated into imperative code. After implementation, the control flow can be analyzed to determine time and space complexity.

The goal is not simply to write code that produces the correct output. A good DSA implementation should also handle edge cases, maintain clear state transitions, use appropriate data structures, and scale reasonably as the input grows.

topics.title: Object-Oriented Concepts
topics.description: Understand the fundamental concepts of object-oriented programming, including classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, interfaces, and composition, and learn how these concepts are used when implementing data structures and algorithms.

sections.title: What is object-oriented programming?
sections.content:
Object-oriented programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm that organizes software around objects. An object combines data with the operations that can be performed on that data.

A class defines the structure and behavior of objects, while an object is an instance created from a class. OOP provides concepts such as encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, and polymorphism that help developers organize larger programs.

Object-oriented programming is particularly useful when implementing data structures because structures such as linked lists, trees, graphs, stacks, and queues can be represented using classes and objects.

OOP concepts in DSA implementations
Why object-oriented concepts matter in DSA
sections.content:
DSA is primarily concerned with organizing data and solving problems efficiently, but those concepts still need to be implemented using a programming language. Object-oriented programming provides useful mechanisms for representing data structures and organizing their operations.

Classes and objects help represent individual components. Encapsulation protects internal state. Abstraction provides simpler interfaces. Polymorphism allows different implementations to be used through common contracts. Composition allows complex structures to be built from smaller components.

You do not need to master advanced OOP design patterns before learning DSA. A strong understanding of classes, objects, encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, and composition is generally sufficient for understanding and implementing most object-oriented DSA examples.

The main goal is to use OOP concepts to make the implementation clear and maintainable while keeping the underlying algorithm easy to understand and analyze.

topics.title: Pseudocode
topics.description: Learn how pseudocode is used to describe algorithms in a simple, language-independent way, including variables, conditions, loops, functions, data structures, and step-by-step problem-solving logic.

sections.title: What is pseudocode?
sections.content:
Pseudocode is an informal way of describing the steps of an algorithm using a mixture of natural language and programming-like instructions. It is designed to communicate the logic of a solution without following the exact syntax of a particular programming language.

Pseudocode allows developers to focus on the problem-solving process before worrying about implementation details such as Java syntax, Python syntax, or library-specific APIs.

For example, a simple algorithm for finding the largest value in an array can be described as:

```text
START
    SET max = first element of the array

    FOR each element in the array
        IF element is greater than max
            SET max = element
        END IF
    END FOR

    RETURN max
END
```

The pseudocode explains the algorithm clearly without depending on a specific programming language.

sections.title: Why use pseudocode?
sections.content:
Pseudocode helps separate algorithmic thinking from programming language syntax. When solving a DSA problem, it is often useful to determine the logical steps first and then translate those steps into code.

Pseudocode can make a solution easier to review, discuss, modify, and explain. It is also useful during technical interviews because a candidate can communicate the approach before writing the complete implementation.

For example, instead of immediately writing Java code for searching an array, the algorithm can first be expressed as:

```text
START
    FOR each element in the array
        IF element equals target
            RETURN its index
        END IF
    END FOR

    RETURN -1
END
```

Once the logic is correct, it can be converted into Java, Python, C++, or another programming language.

sections.title: Pseudocode is language-independent
sections.content:
One of the main advantages of pseudocode is that it does not depend on the syntax of a specific programming language. The same algorithm can be described once and then implemented in different languages.

For example, the following pseudocode describes a linear search:

```text
FUNCTION linearSearch(array, target)
    FOR i FROM 0 TO length(array) - 1
        IF array[i] equals target
            RETURN i
        END IF
    END FOR

    RETURN -1
END FUNCTION
```

The same logic can later be implemented using Java, Python, C++, JavaScript, or another language. The syntax changes, but the underlying algorithm remains the same.

sections.title: Variables in pseudocode
sections.content:
Variables in pseudocode represent values that an algorithm needs to store or update. Unlike programming languages, pseudocode does not require a strict syntax for declaring variable types.

For example:

```text
SET count = 0
SET total = 0

FOR each number in the array
    SET total = total + number
    SET count = count + 1
END FOR
```

The variables count and total maintain information while the algorithm executes.

The exact keywords used for assignment can vary between pseudocode styles. The important goal is to make the meaning of the operation clear.

sections.title: Conditional statements
sections.content:
Pseudocode can represent decisions using IF, ELSE IF, and ELSE statements. These structures describe which operations should be performed when specific conditions are true.

For example:

```text
IF number > 0
    PRINT "Positive"
ELSE IF number < 0
    PRINT "Negative"
ELSE
    PRINT "Zero"
END IF
```

The syntax is intentionally simple. The reader can understand the decision-making logic without needing to know the syntax of a particular programming language.

Conditional statements are essential in DSA because algorithms frequently compare values, check boundaries, handle special cases, and select different processing paths.

sections.title: Loops in pseudocode
sections.content:
Loops describe repeated operations in an algorithm. Pseudocode can use constructs such as FOR, WHILE, and REPEAT to represent repetition.

For example, an algorithm that prints every element in an array can be written as:

```text
FOR each element in the array
    PRINT element
END FOR
```

A loop with an explicit index can also be written as:

```text
FOR i FROM 0 TO length(array) - 1
    PRINT array[i]
END FOR
```

The exact syntax is flexible as long as the beginning, condition, repeated operation, and termination are understandable.

sections.title: WHILE loops
sections.content:
A WHILE loop is useful when repetition should continue as long as a condition remains true. It is particularly useful for algorithms where the number of iterations is not known in advance.

For example, binary search can be expressed using a WHILE loop:

```text
SET left = 0
SET right = length(array) - 1

WHILE left <= right
    SET middle = (left + right) / 2

    IF array[middle] equals target
        RETURN middle
    ELSE IF array[middle] < target
        SET left = middle + 1
    ELSE
        SET right = middle - 1
    END IF
END WHILE

RETURN -1
```

This pseudocode clearly communicates the algorithm without requiring language-specific syntax.

sections.title: Functions in pseudocode
sections.content:
Functions allow pseudocode to divide an algorithm into smaller reusable operations. A function can receive parameters and return a result.

For example:

```text
FUNCTION findMaximum(array)
    SET max = array[0]

    FOR each number in array
        IF number > max
            SET max = number
        END IF
    END FOR

    RETURN max
END FUNCTION
```

The function describes a complete operation without specifying how it must be implemented in a particular programming language.

Breaking complex algorithms into functions can make the overall solution easier to understand and maintain.

sections.title: Arrays and collections in pseudocode
sections.content:
Pseudocode can describe operations on arrays and other collections without committing to a specific programming language's collection API.

For example, finding the sum of all elements can be expressed as:

```text
FUNCTION calculateSum(array)
    SET sum = 0

    FOR each element in array
        SET sum = sum + element
    END FOR

    RETURN sum
END FUNCTION
```

Similarly, an algorithm can describe adding, removing, searching, or updating elements without specifying whether the implementation will use an array, list, set, map, or another data structure.

This allows the algorithmic idea to remain separate from implementation-specific details.

sections.title: Nested loops in pseudocode
sections.content:
Pseudocode can represent nested loops when an algorithm needs to perform repeated operations at multiple levels.

For example, checking every pair of elements in an array can be described as:

```text
FOR i FROM 0 TO length(array) - 1
    FOR j FROM i + 1 TO length(array) - 1
        PROCESS array[i] and array[j]
    END FOR
END FOR
```

This structure is common in problems involving comparisons between pairs of elements.

Nested loops are also important when analyzing complexity. Depending on the loop boundaries, such an algorithm may have O(n²) time complexity.

sections.title: Pseudocode for data structures
sections.content:
Pseudocode can describe operations on data structures without requiring a complete programming-language implementation. This is useful when designing or explaining structures such as stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, and graphs.

For example, stack operations can be described as:

```text
PUSH(value)
    IF stack is full
        REPORT overflow
    ELSE
        ADD value to top of stack
    END IF
END PUSH

POP()
    IF stack is empty
        REPORT underflow
    ELSE
        REMOVE and RETURN top value
    END IF
END POP
```

The pseudocode focuses on what the operations should accomplish rather than the exact syntax or storage mechanism used by the implementation.

sections.title: Pseudocode for recursion
sections.content:
Pseudocode is useful for expressing recursive algorithms because it makes the base case and recursive step easy to identify.

For example, factorial can be represented as:

```text
FUNCTION factorial(n)
    IF n <= 1
        RETURN 1
    END IF

    RETURN n * factorial(n - 1)
END FUNCTION
```

The base case stops the recursion when n reaches 1 or below. The recursive case reduces the problem by calling the same function with n - 1.

Clearly identifying the base case and recursive step is essential when designing recursive algorithms.

sections.title: Pseudocode for sorting
sections.content:
Sorting algorithms can be described using pseudocode before they are implemented in a programming language. For example, a simplified bubble sort can be represented as:

```text
FUNCTION bubbleSort(array)
    FOR i FROM 0 TO length(array) - 1
        FOR j FROM 0 TO length(array) - i - 2
            IF array[j] > array[j + 1]
                SWAP array[j] and array[j + 1]
            END IF
        END FOR
    END FOR

    RETURN array
END FUNCTION
```

This representation makes the algorithm's main idea clear: compare adjacent elements and swap them when they are in the wrong order.

The implementation can later be translated into Java, Python, C++, or another language.

sections.title: Pseudocode and complexity analysis
sections.content:
Pseudocode can also be used to analyze the complexity of an algorithm before writing the final implementation.

For example:

```text
FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
    PROCESS array[i]
END FOR
```

The loop executes n times, so the time complexity is O(n).

For nested loops:

```text
FOR i FROM 0 TO n - 1
    FOR j FROM 0 TO n - 1
        PROCESS i and j
    END FOR
END FOR
```

The inner operation executes approximately n times for each of the n outer iterations, resulting in O(n²) time complexity.

This makes pseudocode useful not only for explaining an algorithm but also for reasoning about its efficiency.

sections.title: Pseudocode to code conversion
Good pseudocode practices
sections.content:
Good pseudocode should be clear, concise, and focused on the algorithm rather than programming-language syntax. The reader should be able to understand the solution without needing to know a specific programming language.

Useful practices include using meaningful variable names, keeping indentation consistent, clearly identifying conditions and loops, separating major steps, and explicitly describing inputs and outputs.

For example:

```text
FUNCTION findIndex(array, target)
    FOR i FROM 0 TO length(array) - 1
        IF array[i] equals target
            RETURN i
        END IF
    END FOR

    RETURN -1
END FUNCTION
```

This is easier to understand than pseudocode that uses unexplained variables or language-specific syntax.

sections.title: Why pseudocode matters in DSA
sections.content:
Pseudocode is an important problem-solving tool in DSA because it allows you to design and verify an algorithm before writing complete code. It encourages you to think about the input, output, processing steps, edge cases, and complexity independently of programming syntax.

A useful workflow is to first understand the problem, identify the required data structures, write the algorithm in pseudocode, analyze its time and space complexity, and then implement it in the chosen programming language.

This approach reduces the chance of getting distracted by syntax while the algorithm itself is still being designed. It also makes it easier to explain a solution during technical interviews and collaborate with other developers.

modules.title: Linked Lists
modules.description: Learn linked lists with clear concepts, examples, implementation thinking, and complexity analysis.

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.description: Understand linked lists, how nodes and references are used to store connected elements, and how to perform traversal, insertion, deletion, searching, and other common linked-list operations while analyzing their time and space complexity.

sections.title: What is a linked list?
sections.content:
A linked list is a linear data structure in which elements are stored in separate objects called nodes. Each node contains data and one or more references that connect it to other nodes.

Unlike an array, linked-list elements do not need to occupy consecutive memory locations. Each node stores a reference to the next node, allowing the nodes to form a sequence.

A simple singly linked list can be represented as:

```text
10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → null
```

The first node is usually called the head. Each node points to the next node, and the final node points to null, indicating the end of the list.

Linked lists are useful when elements need to be inserted or removed without requiring the elements after them to be shifted as they would be in an array.

sections.title: Structure of a linked-list node
Creating a linked list
Traversing a linked list
Inserting at the beginning
sections.content:
Inserting a new node at the beginning of a singly linked list is an efficient operation. The new node points to the current head, and then head is updated to point to the new node.

For example, starting with:

```text
10 → 20 → 30 → null
```

To insert 5 at the beginning:

```java
Node newNode = new Node(5);
newNode.next = head;
head = newNode;
```

The result is:

```text
5 → 10 → 20 → 30 → null
```

The operation requires a constant number of reference changes, so inserting at the beginning takes O(1) time.

sections.title: Inserting at the end
Inserting at a specific position
sections.content:
A node can be inserted at a particular position by traversing to the node immediately before the insertion point and changing the appropriate references.

Suppose the list is:

```text
10 → 20 → 40 → null
```

To insert 30 between 20 and 40:

```text
newNode.next = current.next
current.next = newNode
```

The resulting list is:

```text
10 → 20 → 30 → 40 → null
```

In Java:

```java
Node newNode = new Node(30);

newNode.next = current.next;
current.next = newNode;
```

The reference to the remainder of the list must be preserved before changing current.next. Otherwise, the rest of the list could become inaccessible.

sections.title: Deleting the first node
sections.content:
Deleting the first node of a singly linked list requires moving the head reference to the second node.

For example:

```text
Before:
10 → 20 → 30 → null

After deleting 10:
20 → 30 → null
```

The operation can be implemented as:

```java
if (head != null) {
    head = head.next;
}
```

Only one reference needs to be updated, so deletion from the beginning takes O(1) time.

If the list becomes empty after deletion, head becomes null.

sections.title: Deleting the last node
Searching in a linked list
Finding the length of a linked list
Reversing a singly linked list
Singly linked lists
sections.content:
A singly linked list is the simplest common form of linked list. Each node contains a value and a reference to the next node.

```text
head
 ↓
10 → 20 → 30 → null
```

Each node can move only in the forward direction. Starting from a node, there is no direct reference to its previous node.

Singly linked lists use less memory per node than doubly linked lists because each node stores only one link. They are suitable when operations primarily require forward traversal.

sections.title: Doubly linked lists
Circular linked lists
Linked list vs array
Time complexity of common linked-list operations
sections.content:
The performance of linked-list operations depends on the type of list and which references are available.

For a singly linked list with only a head reference, common complexities are:

```text
Operation                         Complexity
------------------------------------------------
Access by index                  O(n)
Search                           O(n)
Insert at beginning              O(1)
Delete from beginning            O(1)
Insert at end                    O(n)
Delete from end                  O(n)
Traverse                         O(n)

With a tail reference, insertion at the end can be O(1), although deleting the final node from a singly linked list still generally requires finding its predecessor.

These complexities explain why linked lists are useful for some workloads but less suitable for applications that require frequent random access.

sections.title: Common linked-list mistakes
Why linked lists matter in DSA
sections.content:
Linked lists are an important DSA topic because they introduce the idea of storing elements as connected nodes rather than relying on contiguous indexed storage. They also provide practical experience with references and pointer-like relationships between objects.

Understanding linked lists prepares you for more advanced structures such as doubly linked lists, circular lists, trees, graphs, and other structures that rely on references between nodes.

The most important concepts to understand are how nodes are connected, how traversal works, how references change during insertion and deletion, and how these operations affect time and space complexity.

Once these fundamentals are clear, linked lists become a useful foundation for understanding more complex data structures.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how linked lists store connected nodes, how to traverse and modify them, the differences between singly, doubly, and circular lists, and the complexity of common operations.

topics.title: Binary Search Tree
topics.description: Understand Binary Search Trees, their structure, ordering rules, traversal techniques, insertion, searching, deletion, and the performance trade-offs that make BSTs useful for maintaining ordered data.

sections.title: What Is a Binary Search Tree?
sections.content:
A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree in which every node follows an ordering rule. For a given node, values smaller than the node are stored in its left subtree, while values greater than the node are stored in its right subtree.

This ordering makes searching more efficient than searching an unordered binary tree because each comparison tells us which side of the tree may contain the required value.

For example, if the current node contains 50 and we are searching for 30, we know immediately that 30 must be somewhere in the left subtree if it exists.

A BST is therefore a combination of two ideas: a binary tree structure and an ordering property.

sections.title: Structure of a Binary Search Tree
BST Ordering Property
sections.content:
The most important rule of a Binary Search Tree is its ordering property.

For every node:

- Values in the left subtree are smaller than the node's value.
- Values in the right subtree are greater than the node's value.
- The same rule must also be true recursively for every subtree.

Consider this tree:

```text
        50
       /  \
     30    70
    /  \   /  \
   20  40 60  80
```

For node 50, everything in the left subtree is smaller than 50 and everything in the right subtree is greater than 50. The same rule is true for nodes 30 and 70 and their respective subtrees.

sections.title: Creating a Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
A BST can be created by starting with an empty root and inserting values one at a time. The first value normally becomes the root.

For example, inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, and 80 produces:

```text
        50
       /  \
     30    70
    /  \   /  \
   20  40 60  80
```

The insertion position is determined by comparing the new value with the current node.

sections.title: Searching in a Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
Searching is one of the main advantages of a BST. Start at the root and compare the target value with the current node.

If the target equals the current value, the search is successful. If the target is smaller, move to the left child. If it is larger, move to the right child.

For example, searching for 60 in the tree above follows this path:

```text
50 → 70 → 60
```

At each step, an entire subtree can be eliminated from consideration.

sections.title: Searching with Java
Iterative BST Search
Inserting into a Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
To insert a new value, begin at the root and compare the value with each node. Move left when the new value is smaller and right when it is larger. Continue until an empty child position is found.

For example, inserting 35 into the tree:

```text
        50
       /  \
     30    70
    /  \
   20  40
       /
      35
```

The path is 50 → 30 → 40 → 35.

sections.title: BST Insertion in Java
Finding the Minimum Value
Finding the Maximum Value
Inorder Traversal of a BST
sections.content:
Inorder traversal visits nodes in the order: left subtree, current node, right subtree.

One special property of a BST is that inorder traversal produces the values in sorted order.

For this tree:

```text
        50
       /  \
     30    70
    /  \   /  \
   20  40 60  80
```

The inorder traversal is:

```text
20 30 40 50 60 70 80
```

This property is frequently used when a program needs the values of a BST in ascending order.

sections.title: Preorder and Postorder Traversal
sections.content:
BSTs also support the standard binary-tree traversals.

Preorder visits the current node before its children: root, left, right.

Postorder visits the children before the current node: left, right, root.

For the tree with values 50, 30, 70, 20, 40, 60, and 80:

```text
Preorder:  50 30 20 40 70 60 80
Postorder: 20 40 30 60 80 70 50
```

Unlike inorder traversal, preorder and postorder do not generally produce sorted output.

sections.title: Deleting a Leaf Node
sections.content:
Deletion is more complicated than searching or insertion because removing a node can affect the tree structure.

The simplest case is deleting a leaf node, which has no children.

For example, deleting 20 from:

```text
    30
   /  \
 20   40
```

simply removes the reference to 20. Node 30's left child becomes null.

sections.title: Deleting a Node with One Child
sections.content:
If the node being deleted has exactly one child, its parent can be connected directly to that child.

For example:

```text
    30
   /
 20
   \
   25
```

If 20 is deleted, node 30 can point directly to 25:

```text
    30
   /
 25
```

The child effectively takes the deleted node's position.

sections.title: Deleting a Node with Two Children
sections.content:
Deleting a node with two children requires replacing its value while preserving the BST ordering property.

A common approach is to find the inorder successor, which is the smallest value in the node's right subtree. Replace the deleted node's value with that successor value, then delete the successor from its original position.

For example, if 50 has two children, the smallest value in its right subtree can replace 50.

Another valid approach is to use the inorder predecessor, which is the largest value in the left subtree.

sections.title: BST Deletion in Java
Balanced vs Skewed BST
sections.content:
The performance of a BST depends heavily on its shape.

A reasonably balanced tree has a height close to log₂(n), allowing search, insertion, and deletion to operate efficiently.

A skewed tree can occur when values are inserted in an already sorted order. For example, inserting 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 can produce:

```text
10
  \
   20
     \
      30
        \
         40
           \
            50
```

This structure behaves much like a linked list. In that situation, operations can take linear time.

This is why self-balancing trees such as AVL trees and Red-Black trees are used when predictable logarithmic performance is required.

sections.title: Time and Space Complexity
sections.content:
Let h represent the height of the BST.

Search, insertion, and deletion generally take O(h) time because they follow a single path from the root toward a leaf.

For a balanced BST, h is approximately O(log n), so these operations are approximately O(log n).

For a highly skewed BST, h can become O(n), making the operations O(n).

Inorder, preorder, and postorder traversals visit every node, so they take O(n) time.

Recursive implementations also use O(h) call-stack space. An iterative search uses O(1) auxiliary space.

sections.title: Binary Tree vs Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
A binary tree only requires each node to have at most two children. It does not require values to follow a particular ordering.

A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree with an additional ordering constraint.

For example, this is a valid binary tree but not necessarily a valid BST:

```text
      50
     /  \
   70    30
```

The left child is greater than 50 and the right child is smaller, so it violates the BST ordering rule.

sections.title: Common BST Mistakes
sections.content:
Several mistakes commonly appear when implementing BSTs.

First, developers may confuse a binary tree with a BST and forget the ordering property. Second, insertion logic may update the wrong child reference. Third, deletion of a node with two children may be implemented without correctly preserving the ordering property.

Another common mistake is assuming every BST operation is always O(log n). That is only true when the tree height is logarithmic. An ordinary BST can become skewed and degrade to O(n).

Duplicate values also require a deliberate design decision. A BST implementation should define whether duplicates are ignored, counted, or consistently stored on one side.

sections.title: Why Binary Search Trees Matter
sections.content:
Binary Search Trees introduce an important idea in data structures: maintaining data in an ordered structure so that searching and updates can follow a small portion of the data instead of scanning everything.

BST concepts are also the foundation for understanding more advanced ordered-tree structures such as AVL trees and Red-Black trees.

They are useful for learning how ordering, recursion, tree height, traversal, and dynamic insertion and deletion work together. Understanding the strengths and weaknesses of an ordinary BST also makes it easier to understand why self-balancing trees are needed in performance-sensitive systems.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how Binary Search Trees organize values and support efficient searching, insertion, deletion, and sorted traversal.

topics.title: Heap
topics.description: Learn how heaps organize elements using a priority-based tree structure, how min-heaps and max-heaps work, how heaps are represented using arrays, and how insertion, deletion, heapify, and heap sort are implemented.

sections.title: What Is a Heap?
sections.content:
A Heap is a specialized tree-based data structure commonly used when we need quick access to the smallest or largest element.

A heap is a complete binary tree that follows a specific ordering rule called the heap property. There are two common types: a min-heap and a max-heap.

In a min-heap, every parent is smaller than or equal to its children. Therefore, the smallest element is always at the root.

In a max-heap, every parent is greater than or equal to its children. Therefore, the largest element is always at the root.

Unlike a Binary Search Tree, a heap does not keep all values on the left smaller and all values on the right larger. Only the parent-child relationship is guaranteed.

sections.title: Complete Binary Tree
sections.content:
A heap must be a complete binary tree. This means every level is completely filled except possibly the last level, and nodes in the last level are filled from left to right.

For example:

```text
        10
       /  \
      20   30
     / \   /
    40 50 60
```

This is complete because there are no gaps between nodes on the last level.

The complete-tree property is important because it allows a heap to be stored efficiently inside an array without requiring separate node objects or child references.

sections.title: Min-Heap
sections.content:
A min-heap keeps the smallest value at the root. Every parent must be smaller than or equal to its children.

For example:

```text
        10
       /  \
      20   15
     / \   /
    40 30 50
```

The root contains 10, which is the smallest value in the heap. However, the entire tree is not sorted. For example, 20 can be greater than 15 even though 20 appears before 15 in the tree.

The heap property only requires each parent to be smaller than or equal to its children.

sections.title: Max-Heap
sections.content:
A max-heap is the opposite of a min-heap. Every parent must be greater than or equal to its children.

Example:

```text
        50
       /  \
      40   45
     / \   /
    10 30 20
```

The largest value is always available at the root. Like a min-heap, a max-heap is not completely sorted. The heap property only applies between a node and its children.

sections.title: Heap Representation Using an Array
sections.content:
Because a heap is a complete binary tree, it can be efficiently represented using an array.

For a zero-based array, if a node is stored at index i:

- Left child = 2 * i + 1
- Right child = 2 * i + 2
- Parent = (i - 1) / 2

For example, this heap:

```text
        10
       /  \
      20   30
     / \   /
    40 50 60
```

can be represented as:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
```

No explicit left or right references are required.

sections.title: Finding Parent and Children
sections.content:
The array representation makes navigation between parent and child nodes a simple arithmetic calculation.

For an element at index 2:

```text
left child  = 2 * 2 + 1 = 5
right child = 2 * 2 + 2 = 6
parent      = (2 - 1) / 2 = 0
```

The integer division used for the parent calculation gives index 0.

This representation is one of the main reasons heaps are usually implemented with arrays rather than linked tree nodes.

sections.title: Heap Insertion
sections.content:
When inserting an element into a heap, the new value is first placed at the end of the array. This preserves the complete binary tree structure.

After that, the value is compared with its parent. If the heap property is violated, the new value is swapped with its parent. This process continues until the correct position is found.

This operation is called sift up, bubble up, or heapify up.

sections.title: Min-Heap Insertion Example
sections.content:
Suppose we have this min-heap:

```text
        10
       /  \
      20   30
     / \
    40 50
```

Now insert 5. It is first placed at the next available position:

```text
        10
       /  \
      20   30
     / \   /
    40 50 5
```

Since 5 is smaller than its parent 30, swap them. Then compare 5 with 10 and swap again.

The final heap becomes:

```text
         5
       /   \
     20     10
    /  \   /
   40  50 30
```

sections.title: Heap Insertion in Java
Removing the Root
sections.content:
The root is the most important element in a heap. In a min-heap it is the minimum value, while in a max-heap it is the maximum value.

To remove the root, the last element in the array is moved to the root position. The last element is then removed from the array.

Moving the last element to the root preserves the complete-tree structure, but it may violate the heap property. Therefore, the element must be moved downward until the heap property is restored.

This process is called sift down, bubble down, or heapify down.

sections.title: Heapify Down
sections.content:
For a min-heap, heapify down compares the current node with its children and swaps it with the smaller child when necessary.

For a max-heap, it swaps with the larger child instead.

For example, suppose a min-heap root contains 50 while its children contain 20 and 30. The root violates the heap property, so 50 must be swapped with 20 because 20 is the smaller child.

The process continues until the node is smaller than both children or reaches a leaf.

sections.title: Removing Root in Java
Peek Operation
Building a Heap from an Array
sections.content:
A heap can be built from an existing unsorted array. One approach is to insert every element individually, but there is a more efficient technique called bottom-up heap construction.

The process starts from the last non-leaf node and performs heapify down toward the root.

For a zero-based array of size n, the last non-leaf node is at index:

```text
n / 2 - 1
```

All nodes after this position are leaves and already satisfy the heap property by themselves.

sections.title: Build Heap in Java
Heap Sort
sections.content:
Heap sort uses the heap structure to sort an array. For ascending order, a max-heap can be built first. The largest value is then repeatedly moved to the end of the array, and the remaining portion is heapified again.

The high-level process is:

```text
1. Build a max-heap.
2. Swap the root with the last element.
3. Reduce the active heap size.
4. Heapify down from the root.
5. Repeat until the array is sorted.
```

Heap sort has O(n log n) time complexity and can be performed in-place.

sections.title: Priority Queue and Heap
sections.content:
A priority queue is an abstract data type where elements are removed according to priority rather than insertion order.

A heap is one of the most common data structures used to implement a priority queue.

For example, a min-heap can implement a priority queue where the smallest priority number is processed first. A max-heap can implement one where the largest priority value is processed first.

In Java, the standard PriorityQueue class uses heap-based behavior internally and provides efficient insertion and removal of the highest-priority element.

sections.title: Heap in Java Using PriorityQueue
Max-Heap Using PriorityQueue
Heap vs Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
A heap and a Binary Search Tree are both tree-based structures, but they solve different problems.

A BST maintains an ordering relationship across left and right subtrees. This makes it useful for ordered searching and operations such as finding predecessor and successor.

A heap only guarantees the parent-child heap property. It is especially useful when we repeatedly need the minimum or maximum element.

For example, finding the minimum in a min-heap is O(1), while finding an arbitrary value is not generally O(log n). In a balanced BST, searching for a specific value can be O(log n).

sections.title: Heap Time Complexity
sections.content:
The main heap operations have predictable complexity.

For a binary heap:

- Peek: O(1)
- Insert: O(log n)
- Remove root: O(log n)
- Heapify down: O(log n)
- Heapify up: O(log n)
- Build heap: O(n)
- Heap sort: O(n log n)

The logarithmic operations come from the height of a complete binary tree, which is O(log n).

A heap typically requires O(n) space to store n elements.

sections.title: Common Heap Mistakes
sections.content:
One common mistake is assuming that a heap is a completely sorted structure. It is not. Only the heap property between parents and children is guaranteed.

Another mistake is using the wrong child when performing heapify down. In a min-heap, the current node should generally be swapped with the smaller child; in a max-heap, it should be swapped with the larger child.

Developers also sometimes forget that the array formulas depend on zero-based indexing. For zero-based arrays, the left child is 2 * i + 1 and the right child is 2 * i + 2.

Finally, removing an arbitrary element from a heap requires additional handling and is different from removing the root.

sections.title: Why Heaps Matter
sections.content:
Heaps are important because they provide efficient access to the highest- or lowest-priority element while supporting dynamic insertion and removal.

They are widely used to implement priority queues and are fundamental to algorithms such as heap sort, Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm, and several scheduling and top-k problems.

Understanding heaps also builds a strong foundation for solving interview problems involving priorities, repeatedly selecting the smallest or largest value, merging sorted data, and maintaining a changing set of candidates.

topics.title: Sets
topics.description: Learn how sets store unique elements, how to perform common set operations, how hash-based and tree-based sets work, and how sets are used to solve duplicate, membership, and collection problems efficiently.

sections.title: What Is a Set?
sections.content:
A Set is a collection that stores unique elements. Unlike a list or array, a set does not normally allow duplicate values.

For example, if we try to store:

```text
[10, 20, 10, 30, 20]
```

a set contains only:

```text
[10, 20, 30]
```

The main purpose of a set is to efficiently determine whether a value exists and to maintain a collection of distinct elements.

Sets are especially useful for removing duplicates, checking membership, tracking visited elements, and performing mathematical set operations.

sections.title: Properties of Sets
sections.content:
A set generally has three important characteristics.

First, duplicate elements are not stored. Second, membership is the primary operation, meaning we frequently ask whether an element exists. Third, the ordering behavior depends on the implementation.

For example, a hash-based set does not guarantee sorted iteration order, while a tree-based set maintains elements according to an ordering rule.

Therefore, choosing the right set implementation depends on whether the application needs fast membership checks, predictable insertion order, or sorted elements.

sections.title: Creating a Set in Java
Adding Elements to a Set
Checking Membership
Removing Elements
Set Size and Empty Check
Iterating Through a Set
Removing Duplicates Using a Set
HashSet
LinkedHashSet
TreeSet
Set Union
Set Intersection
Set Difference
Checking Whether Sets Are Equal
Subset and Superset
Set and Hashing
sections.content:
Hash-based sets use hashing to determine where elements should be stored. When an object is added, its hashCode contributes to determining the internal location used by the set.

When contains or remove is called, the set uses hashing to locate the relevant entry and then uses equality checks to determine whether the exact element exists.

For custom Java classes, hashCode and equals must be implemented consistently. If two objects are considered equal by equals, they must return the same hash code.

sections.title: Sets with Custom Objects
Immutable Sets
sections.content:
Sometimes a program needs a set whose contents should not be changed after creation. Java provides convenient factory methods such as Set.of for creating immutable sets.

```java
Set<String> languages = Set.of("Java", "Python", "Go");

System.out.println(languages.contains("Java"));
```

Attempting to add or remove elements from this set results in an UnsupportedOperationException.

Immutable collections can be useful when data should remain unchanged after initialization.

sections.title: Set Complexity
sections.content:
The complexity of set operations depends on the implementation.

For HashSet, add, remove, and contains are typically O(1) on average.

For LinkedHashSet, these operations are also typically O(1) on average, with additional overhead for maintaining insertion order.

For TreeSet, add, remove, and contains are typically O(log n) because the elements are maintained in a balanced tree.

Iterating through all elements takes O(n) time.

Choosing the implementation should therefore depend on whether the application needs hashing, insertion order, or sorted order.

sections.title: Set vs List
sections.content:
A List is generally used when order and positional access matter, while a Set is used when uniqueness and membership matter.

A list can contain duplicates:

```text
[10, 20, 10, 30]
```

A set removes duplicates:

```text
{10, 20, 30}
```

A List supports operations such as get(index), while a Set does not provide normal index-based access.

If the main requirement is "have I already seen this value?", a set is often a better fit than a list.

sections.title: Common Set Use Cases
Common Set Mistakes
sections.content:
A common mistake is assuming that every Set implementation maintains insertion order. HashSet does not guarantee this behavior.

Another mistake is modifying a set while iterating over it using a normal iterator or enhanced for loop. This can result in ConcurrentModificationException. When elements need to be removed during iteration, use the iterator's remove method or an appropriate collection operation.

Developers should also remember that custom objects require consistent equals and hashCode implementations when used with hash-based sets.

Finally, choosing TreeSet only because it is a Set can be unnecessary if sorted order is not required. HashSet is generally more appropriate when the main requirement is fast membership checking.

sections.title: Why Sets Matter
sections.content:
Sets are one of the most useful collection abstractions because they directly represent the idea of uniqueness.

They allow programs to efficiently answer questions such as whether a value has already appeared, whether two collections share elements, and which values are unique to one collection.

Understanding sets also provides a foundation for hash tables, hashing, graph algorithms, duplicate detection, frequency-related problems, and many common coding-interview patterns.

topics.shortDescription: Learn how sets store unique elements, perform membership checks, remove duplicates, and support union, intersection, difference, and ordered collection operations.

modules.title: Queues
modules.description: Learn queues with clear concepts, examples, implementation thinking, and complexity analysis.

topics.title: Queues
topics.description: Learn how queues organize elements using the First-In, First-Out principle, how to implement queues with arrays and linked lists, and how circular queues, dequeues, and priority queues are used in real-world and algorithmic problems.

sections.title: What Is a Queue?
sections.content:
A Queue is a linear data structure that follows the First-In, First-Out (FIFO) principle. The element that enters the queue first is normally the first element to leave.

A simple real-world example is a line of people waiting at a counter. The person who arrives first is served first.

A queue has two important ends:

- Front: The position from which elements are removed.
- Rear: The position at which new elements are inserted.

For example:

```text
Front                         Rear
  ↓                            ↓
[10] → [20] → [30] → [40]
```

If 50 is added, it is placed at the rear. If an element is removed, 10 leaves from the front.

sections.title: FIFO Principle
sections.content:
FIFO means First-In, First-Out. The first element inserted into the queue is the first element removed.

Suppose we insert the following values:

```text
10 → 20 → 30 → 40
```

The removal order will be:

```text
10 → 20 → 30 → 40
```

This behavior makes queues useful when tasks need to be processed in the same order in which they arrive.

sections.title: Basic Queue Operations
sections.content:
The most common queue operations are enqueue, dequeue, peek, and isEmpty.

Enqueue adds an element to the rear.

Dequeue removes an element from the front.

Peek returns the front element without removing it.

isEmpty checks whether the queue contains any elements.

For example:

```text
Initial:    [10, 20, 30]
Enqueue 40: [10, 20, 30, 40]
Dequeue:    [20, 30, 40]
Peek:       20
```

sections.title: Enqueue Operation
sections.content:
Enqueue is the operation used to add a new element to the rear of the queue.

If the queue contains:

```text
Front → [10] [20] [30] ← Rear
```

and we enqueue 40, the queue becomes:

```text
Front → [10] [20] [30] [40] ← Rear
```

The existing elements do not change position. The new element is simply added at the rear.

sections.title: Dequeue Operation
sections.content:
Dequeue removes and returns the element at the front of the queue.

For example:

```text
Front → [10] [20] [30] ← Rear
```

After dequeue:

```text
Front → [20] [30] ← Rear
```

The element 10 is removed because it was the first element inserted.

sections.title: Peek Operation
Queue Implementation Using Linked List
sections.content:
A queue can be implemented efficiently using a linked list with references to both the front and rear nodes.

```text
Front → [10] → [20] → [30] ← Rear
```

When enqueueing, the new node is attached after the rear node and the rear reference is updated.

When dequeueing, the front reference moves to the next node.

With both front and rear references, enqueue and dequeue can both be performed in O(1) time.

sections.title: Queue Using Linked List in Java
Queue Using an Array
sections.content:
A queue can also be implemented using an array. Two indexes are commonly maintained: one for the front and another for the rear.

A straightforward array implementation may suffer from unused spaces after several dequeue operations if elements are not shifted or the array is not treated as circular.

For example:

```text
Initial:
[10] [20] [30] [40]
 ↑               ↑
front           rear

After two dequeues:
[  ] [  ] [30] [40]
          ↑       ↑
        front    rear
```

The empty positions at the beginning cannot be reused by a simple linear implementation without additional logic.

sections.title: Circular Queue
sections.content:
A Circular Queue solves the unused-space problem of a simple array queue by treating the array as if its end connects back to its beginning.

When the rear reaches the last array position, it can move back to index 0 if there is available space.

The next index is commonly calculated using:

```text
nextIndex = (index + 1) % capacity
```

This allows previously freed positions to be reused without shifting elements.

sections.title: Circular Queue Example
sections.content:
Consider a circular queue with capacity 5:

```text
[10] [20] [30] [40] [50]
```

If 10 and 20 are removed, their positions become available:

```text
[  ] [  ] [30] [40] [50]
```

If another element is inserted, the rear can wrap around and use index 0:

```text
[60] [  ] [30] [40] [50]
```

The logical queue order is still maintained even though the physical array positions wrap around.

sections.title: Circular Queue in Java
Deque
sections.content:
A Deque, pronounced "deck", stands for Double-Ended Queue. It allows insertion and removal from both the front and the rear.

For example:

```text
Front                         Rear
  ↓                            ↓
[10] ↔ [20] ↔ [30] ↔ [40]
```

Elements can be added or removed from either end.

A deque can therefore behave like a queue when operations are restricted to one end for insertion and the other for removal, or like a stack when both operations happen at the same end.

sections.title: Deque in Java
Priority Queue
sections.content:
A Priority Queue is different from a normal FIFO queue. Elements are removed according to their priority rather than simply according to insertion order.

For example, if the smallest value represents the highest priority:

```text
Insert: 30, 10, 20

Removal order:
10 → 20 → 30
```

A heap is commonly used to implement a priority queue efficiently.

In Java, PriorityQueue provides this behavior by default as a min-priority queue.

sections.title: PriorityQueue in Java
Queue in Breadth-First Search
sections.content:
Queues are fundamental to Breadth-First Search (BFS). BFS explores a graph or tree level by level.

When a node is discovered, it is added to the queue. The next node to process is removed from the front.

For example:

```text
        A
       / \
      B   C
     / \
    D   E
```

BFS processes the nodes as:

```text
A → B → C → D → E
```

The queue ensures that nodes discovered earlier are processed before nodes discovered later.

sections.title: BFS Queue Implementation
Queue Applications
sections.content:
Queues are useful whenever work should be processed in arrival order or level order.

Common applications include:

- CPU and task scheduling
- Print-job processing
- Request processing
- Message queues
- Breadth-first search
- Level-order tree traversal
- Producer-consumer systems
- Network packet buffering

For example, a server can place incoming tasks into a queue and process them one at a time in the order they were received.

sections.title: Queue Complexity
sections.content:
A properly implemented queue supports enqueue and dequeue in O(1) time.

For a linked-list implementation with front and rear references:

- Enqueue: O(1)
- Dequeue: O(1)
- Peek: O(1)

For a circular array queue, enqueue, dequeue, and peek are also O(1).

A naive array implementation that shifts every remaining element after dequeue can take O(n), which is why shifting should generally be avoided when implementing an efficient queue.

sections.title: Queue vs Stack
sections.content:
Both queues and stacks are linear data structures, but they process elements differently.

A queue follows FIFO:

```text
First inserted → First removed
```

A stack follows LIFO:

```text
Last inserted → First removed
```

For example, if we insert 10, 20, and 30:

Queue removal order:
```text
10 → 20 → 30
```

Stack removal order:
```text
30 → 20 → 10
```

The correct structure depends on whether the problem requires arrival order or reverse insertion order.

sections.title: Common Queue Mistakes
sections.content:
One common mistake is confusing FIFO queue behavior with LIFO stack behavior.

Another mistake is removing elements from the front of a normal array by shifting every remaining element. This can make dequeue O(n).

When implementing a linked-list queue, developers may also forget to update the rear reference when the last element is removed.

In a circular queue, incorrect handling of front, rear, size, or wrap-around conditions can cause the queue to incorrectly appear full or empty.

It is also important to distinguish a normal FIFO queue from a priority queue because their removal rules are different.

sections.title: Why Queues Matter
sections.content:
Queues provide a simple and powerful way to control the order in which work is processed. Their FIFO behavior naturally models waiting lines, task processing, buffering, and level-by-level traversal.

Understanding queues is essential for graph algorithms such as BFS, tree level-order traversal, scheduling problems, producer-consumer systems, and many interview problems involving ordered processing.

Once the basic queue is understood, circular queues, deques, and priority queues provide additional ways to control how elements enter and leave a data structure.
