topics.title: AVL TREE
topics.description: Learn how AVL trees keep a Binary Search Tree balanced using height and balance factors, how rotations restore balance after insertion and deletion, and why self-balancing trees provide predictable logarithmic performance.

sections.title: What Is an AVL Tree?
sections.content:
An AVL Tree is a self-balancing Binary Search Tree. AVL stands for Adelson-Velsky and Landis, the names of the researchers who introduced the structure.

Like a normal Binary Search Tree, an AVL tree maintains the ordering rule that values smaller than a node are stored in its left subtree and values greater than a node are stored in its right subtree.

The additional requirement is that the tree must remain balanced after insertions and deletions.

For every node, the height difference between its left and right subtrees must be at most 1. When this condition is violated, the tree performs one or more rotations to restore balance.

This prevents the tree from becoming highly skewed and provides O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion in the worst case.

sections.title: Why Do We Need AVL Trees?
sections.content:
A normal Binary Search Tree can become skewed when values are inserted in an unfortunate order.

For example, inserting 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 can produce:

```text
10
  \
   20
     \
      30
        \
         40
           \
            50
```

This structure behaves almost like a linked list. Searching for an element can therefore take O(n) time.

An AVL tree automatically rearranges its structure using rotations so that the height remains logarithmic.

The goal is not to keep the tree perfectly balanced after every operation, but to ensure that no node becomes too far heavier on one side than the other.

sections.title: AVL Tree Balance Property
sections.content:
The defining property of an AVL tree is its balance condition.

For every node:

```text
|height(left subtree) - height(right subtree)| <= 1
```

If the difference is 0, both subtrees have the same height.

If the difference is 1 or -1, the node is still balanced.

If the difference becomes 2 or -2, the node is unbalanced and a rotation is required.

For example:

```text
      30
     /  \
   20    40
```

The left and right subtree heights are equal, so node 30 is balanced.

sections.title: Height of an AVL Tree
Calculating Node Height
Balance Factor
sections.content:
The balance factor tells us whether a node is balanced and which side is heavier.

It is commonly calculated as:

```text
balance factor = height(left subtree) - height(right subtree)
```

For an AVL tree, valid balance factors are:

```text
-1, 0, +1
```

A balance factor of +2 means the left subtree is too tall, while -2 means the right subtree is too tall.

For example, if the left subtree has height 3 and the right subtree has height 1:

```text
balance factor = 3 - 1 = 2
```

The node needs rebalancing.

sections.title: Calculating Balance Factor in Java
AVL Rotations
sections.content:
Rotations are local tree transformations used to restore the AVL balance property while preserving the Binary Search Tree ordering.

There are four common imbalance patterns:

- Left-Left (LL)
- Right-Right (RR)
- Left-Right (LR)
- Right-Left (RL)

LL and RR cases require a single rotation.

LR and RL cases require two rotations.

Rotations change the shape of a subtree without changing the sorted order of its elements.

sections.title: Right Rotation
sections.content:
A right rotation is commonly used to fix a Left-Left imbalance.

Before rotation:

```text
        30
       /
      20
     /
    10
```

After a right rotation around 30:

```text
       20
      /  \
     10   30
```

The BST ordering is preserved, but the tree becomes balanced.

The right child of 20's subtree, if present, is moved to become the left child of 30.

sections.title: Right Rotation in Java
Left Rotation
sections.content:
A left rotation is commonly used to fix a Right-Right imbalance.

Before rotation:

```text
    10
      \
       20
         \
          30
```

After a left rotation around 10:

```text
       20
      /  \
     10   30
```

The ordering property remains unchanged, but the height difference is reduced.

sections.title: Left Rotation in Java
Left-Left Case
sections.content:
The Left-Left case occurs when a node becomes unbalanced because a new value was inserted into the left subtree of its left child.

Example:

```text
        30
       /
      20
     /
    10
```

The balance factor of 30 becomes +2, and the heavy path is left-left.

The solution is a single right rotation:

```text
       20
      /  \
     10   30
```

This is one of the simplest AVL rebalancing cases.

sections.title: Right-Right Case
sections.content:
The Right-Right case occurs when a node becomes unbalanced because a new value was inserted into the right subtree of its right child.

Example:

```text
10
  \
   20
     \
      30
```

The balance factor of 10 becomes -2.

The solution is a single left rotation:

```text
       20
      /  \
     10   30
```

sections.title: Left-Right Case
sections.content:
The Left-Right case occurs when a node is left-heavy, but its left child is right-heavy.

Example:

```text
      30
     /
    10
      \
       20
```

A single right rotation would not correctly solve the imbalance. The solution requires two rotations.

First, perform a left rotation on 10:

```text
      30
     /
    20
   /
  10
```

Then perform a right rotation on 30:

```text
      20
     /  \
    10   30
```

This is called the Left-Right or LR case.

sections.title: Right-Left Case
sections.content:
The Right-Left case is the mirror image of the Left-Right case.

Example:

```text
10
  \
   30
   /
  20
```

The node 10 is right-heavy, but its right child is left-heavy.

First, perform a right rotation on 30:

```text
10
  \
   20
     \
      30
```

Then perform a left rotation on 10:

```text
      20
     /  \
    10   30
```

This combination restores the AVL balance.

sections.title: AVL Rotation Decision Table
sections.content:
The four imbalance cases can be remembered by looking at the direction of the heavy path.

```text
LL → Right Rotation
RR → Left Rotation
LR → Left Rotation on child, then Right Rotation
RL → Right Rotation on child, then Left Rotation
```

Another useful way to think about it is:

- If the imbalance and child direction are the same, use one rotation.
- If they are different, use two rotations.

This pattern becomes especially useful when implementing AVL insertion.

sections.title: AVL Insertion
sections.content:
AVL insertion begins exactly like insertion into a normal Binary Search Tree. The new value is placed according to the BST ordering rule.

After insertion, the algorithm moves back toward the root and updates the height of each ancestor.

For every ancestor, it calculates the balance factor. If the balance factor becomes +2 or -2, the appropriate rotation case is applied.

The important point is that AVL balancing happens after the normal BST insertion. The rotations are then used to repair any imbalance created by the insertion.

sections.title: AVL Insertion in Java
AVL Deletion
sections.content:
Deletion in an AVL tree starts with normal Binary Search Tree deletion.

There are three standard BST deletion cases:

- The node is a leaf.
- The node has one child.
- The node has two children.

After the node is removed, the algorithm moves back toward the root, updates heights, calculates balance factors, and performs rotations when necessary.

Unlike insertion, deletion can cause multiple ancestors to become unbalanced, so rebalancing may need to continue all the way toward the root.

sections.title: AVL Deletion Rebalancing
sections.content:
After deleting a node, the balance factor of an ancestor can become +2 or -2. The correct rotation depends not only on the direction of the imbalance but also on the balance factor of the heavier child.

For example, if a node has balance factor +2, its left subtree is too tall. If the left child has a non-negative balance factor, a right rotation can be appropriate. If the left child is right-heavy, a left rotation on the child followed by a right rotation may be needed.

This makes AVL deletion more involved than AVL insertion, but the same four rotation patterns are still used.

sections.title: Searching in an AVL Tree
sections.content:
Searching in an AVL tree works exactly like searching in a Binary Search Tree.

Compare the target with the current node. If it is smaller, move left. If it is larger, move right. If it matches, the value has been found.

The major difference is that an AVL tree guarantees logarithmic height, so searching remains O(log n) in the worst case.

No special search algorithm is required because the AVL tree preserves the normal BST ordering property.

sections.title: AVL Tree Complexity
sections.content:
The main advantage of an AVL tree is its guaranteed height bound.

For n nodes, the height of an AVL tree is O(log n). Therefore:

- Search: O(log n)
- Insertion: O(log n)
- Deletion: O(log n)
- Rotation: O(1)

A single insertion or deletion may require several height updates, but the total work remains logarithmic because the tree height is logarithmic.

An AVL tree requires O(n) space for its nodes and typically stores an additional height field in each node.

sections.title: AVL Tree vs Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
An AVL tree is a specialized Binary Search Tree that adds a balancing requirement.

A normal BST may have O(log n) operations when its shape is balanced, but it can degrade to O(n) when it becomes skewed.

An AVL tree performs rotations to prevent this degradation and guarantees O(log n) search, insertion, and deletion.

The trade-off is additional implementation complexity. AVL trees must maintain heights, calculate balance factors, and perform rotations after updates.

sections.title: AVL Tree vs Red-Black Tree
sections.content:
AVL trees and Red-Black trees are both self-balancing Binary Search Trees, but they use different balancing rules.

AVL trees maintain a stricter height-balance condition, which can result in shorter trees for some workloads. Red-Black trees use a different set of structural rules and generally perform fewer balancing operations during updates.

Both provide O(log n) worst-case search, insertion, and deletion.

The choice between them depends on the workload and implementation requirements. Java's TreeMap and TreeSet, for example, use a Red-Black tree rather than an AVL tree.

sections.title: Common AVL Tree Mistakes
sections.content:
A common mistake is forgetting to update node heights after a rotation or insertion. Incorrect heights lead to incorrect balance factors and eventually incorrect rotations.

Another common mistake is performing the correct rotation on the wrong node. The rotation must be applied to the first unbalanced ancestor encountered while moving back toward the root.

Developers may also confuse LR and RL cases. The easiest way to distinguish them is to identify whether the heavy path turns direction between the unbalanced node and its child.

Finally, remember that an AVL tree must preserve the BST ordering property after every rotation. A rotation is valid only when it changes the shape without breaking the sorted relationship between nodes.

sections.title: Why AVL Trees Matter
sections.content:
AVL trees demonstrate an important data-structure concept: a structure can automatically reorganize itself to maintain predictable performance.

They combine the ordered-search behavior of a Binary Search Tree with an explicit balancing mechanism. This guarantees that the tree does not degrade into a linked-list-like structure.

Understanding AVL trees is also useful for learning other balanced-tree structures, tree rotations, balance factors, recursive tree updates, and the trade-offs involved in maintaining strict performance guarantees.

topics.title: Sorting
topics.description: Learn how sorting algorithms arrange data into a defined order, understand comparison-based and non-comparison-based sorting, and explore important algorithms such as Bubble Sort, Selection Sort, Insertion Sort, Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Heap Sort, Counting Sort, Radix Sort, and Bucket Sort.

sections.title: What Is Sorting?
sections.content:
Sorting is the process of arranging elements in a specific order. The most common orders are ascending and descending.

For example, an unsorted array:

```text
[40, 10, 30, 20, 50]
```

can be sorted in ascending order as:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
```

Sorting is one of the most fundamental operations in computer science because ordered data can make searching, grouping, comparison, and reporting much easier.

Different sorting algorithms use different strategies and have different time, space, and stability characteristics.

sections.title: Why Sorting Is Important
sections.content:
Sorting appears in many real-world applications and algorithmic problems.

Sorted data can make binary search possible, simplify duplicate detection, make range queries easier, and help organize information for users.

For example, if an array is sorted:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
```

binary search can locate an element without checking every value.

Sorting is also commonly used before solving problems involving intervals, rankings, closest values, merging data, scheduling, and frequency analysis.

sections.title: Ascending and Descending Order
sections.content:
Ascending order arranges values from smaller to larger.

```text
[5, 2, 8, 1, 4]
```

becomes:

```text
[1, 2, 4, 5, 8]
```

Descending order arranges values from larger to smaller:

```text
[8, 5, 4, 2, 1]
```

Most sorting algorithms can be adapted for either direction by changing the comparison condition.

sections.title: Comparison-Based Sorting
sections.content:
Comparison-based sorting algorithms determine the order of elements by comparing pairs of values.

Examples include:

- Bubble Sort
- Selection Sort
- Insertion Sort
- Merge Sort
- Quick Sort
- Heap Sort

For example, an algorithm may compare two values:

```text
20 > 10
```

and use that result to decide whether the elements need to be exchanged.

For general comparison-based sorting, algorithms cannot guarantee better than O(n log n) time in the general case.

sections.title: Bubble Sort
sections.content:
Bubble Sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them when they are in the wrong order.

For example:

```text
[5, 2, 4, 1]
```

The first pass compares adjacent elements and gradually moves the largest value toward the end.

After enough passes, the array becomes sorted.

Bubble Sort is easy to understand and implement, but it is inefficient for large datasets because its average and worst-case time complexity is O(n²).

sections.title: Bubble Sort in Java
Selection Sort
sections.content:
Selection Sort repeatedly finds the smallest element from the unsorted portion and places it at the beginning of that portion.

For example:

```text
[40, 10, 30, 20]
```

The smallest value, 10, is selected and moved to the first position:

```text
[10, 40, 30, 20]
```

The process then continues with the remaining unsorted elements.

Selection Sort performs O(n²) comparisons in the best, average, and worst cases.

sections.title: Selection Sort in Java
Insertion Sort
sections.content:
Insertion Sort builds the sorted portion of an array one element at a time.

It works similarly to how people often arrange playing cards in their hand. Take the next value and insert it into the correct position among the values that are already sorted.

For example:

```text
[10, 20, 40, 30]
```

The value 30 is inserted between 20 and 40:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40]
```

Insertion Sort has O(n²) average and worst-case complexity, but it can run in O(n) time when the input is already sorted or nearly sorted.

sections.title: Insertion Sort in Java
Merge Sort
sections.content:
Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm. It repeatedly divides the array into smaller parts, sorts those parts, and then merges the sorted parts.

For example:

```text
[38, 27, 43, 3]
```

is divided into:

```text
[38, 27]    [43, 3]
```

then:

```text
[38] [27]    [43] [3]
```

The smaller arrays are sorted and merged until the complete array is sorted.

Merge Sort has O(n log n) time complexity in the best, average, and worst cases.

sections.title: Merge Sort in Java
Quick Sort
sections.content:
Quick Sort is another divide-and-conquer algorithm. It selects a pivot and partitions the array so that elements smaller than the pivot are placed on one side and larger elements are placed on the other side.

The process is then repeated recursively for the two partitions.

For example:

```text
[7, 2, 9, 4, 1]
```

If 4 is selected as the pivot, the values can be partitioned into groups containing values smaller and larger than 4.

Quick Sort has O(n log n) average-case time complexity, but its worst-case complexity is O(n) when partitions repeatedly become highly unbalanced.

sections.title: Quick Sort in Java
Heap Sort
sections.content:
Heap Sort uses a heap to repeatedly select the largest or smallest remaining element.

For ascending order, a max-heap is commonly used. The largest value is moved to the end of the array, the heap size is reduced, and the remaining elements are heapified again.

Heap Sort has O(n log n) time complexity in the best, average, and worst cases.

It can also be implemented in-place, requiring only O(1) auxiliary space apart from the input array.

sections.title: Counting Sort
sections.content:
Counting Sort is a non-comparison-based sorting algorithm that works well when the input values belong to a relatively small integer range.

Instead of comparing elements, it counts how many times each value occurs.

For example:

```text
Input: [2, 1, 3, 2, 1]

Counts:
1 → 2
2 → 2
3 → 1
```

The counts can then be used to reconstruct the sorted array:

```text
[1, 1, 2, 2, 3]
```

Its time complexity is O(n + k), where k represents the range of values. It is not generally suitable when the value range is extremely large compared with the number of elements.

sections.title: Counting Sort in Java
Radix Sort
sections.content:
Radix Sort sorts numbers by processing their digits one position at a time rather than comparing complete values.

For decimal numbers, it can process the ones digit first, followed by tens, hundreds, and so on.

For example:

```text
[170, 45, 75, 90, 802, 24, 2, 66]
```

The algorithm repeatedly groups elements according to the current digit while preserving the order produced by previous passes.

Radix Sort is commonly implemented with a stable sorting method such as Counting Sort for each digit position.

Its complexity can be expressed as O(d(n + k)), where d is the number of digit positions and k is the digit range.

sections.title: Bucket Sort
sections.content:
Bucket Sort distributes elements into several buckets, sorts each bucket individually, and then combines the buckets.

For example, values between 0 and 1 can be distributed into buckets representing ranges:

```text
0.0 - 0.2
0.2 - 0.4
0.4 - 0.6
0.6 - 0.8
0.8 - 1.0
```

The effectiveness of Bucket Sort depends heavily on how evenly the input values are distributed.

With suitable input distribution, its average performance can approach O(n), although its worst-case complexity can be O(n²) depending on the sorting method used inside the buckets.

sections.title: Stable Sorting
sections.content:
A sorting algorithm is stable if two elements with equal keys maintain their relative order after sorting.

Consider employees sorted by salary:

```text
(Amit, 50000)
(Neha, 50000)
(Ravi, 60000)
```

If the original order of Amit and Neha matters, a stable sort keeps Amit before Neha when their salaries are equal.

Stability is especially useful when sorting objects by multiple fields. A stable sort can preserve the ordering established by an earlier sorting operation.

sections.title: In-Place Sorting
sections.content:
An in-place sorting algorithm uses a small amount of additional memory relative to the input size and performs most of its work directly inside the original array.

Examples include typical implementations of:

- Selection Sort
- Insertion Sort
- Heap Sort
- Quick Sort

Merge Sort for arrays generally requires O(n) auxiliary memory for merging.

In-place does not necessarily mean that an algorithm uses absolutely zero extra memory. It usually means that the extra space is O(1) or otherwise small compared with the input size.

sections.title: Adaptive Sorting
sections.content:
An adaptive sorting algorithm takes advantage of existing order in the input.

Insertion Sort is a classic example. If the array is already sorted, it can complete in O(n) time because very few shifts are required.

For example:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
```

requires very little work for Insertion Sort.

Adaptive algorithms can therefore be useful when the input is known to be partially sorted or nearly sorted.

sections.title: Sorting Algorithm Comparison
sections.content:
Different sorting algorithms are appropriate for different situations.

```text
Algorithm       Best        Average      Worst       Extra Space
Bubble Sort     O(n)        O(n²)        O(n²)       O(1)
Selection Sort  O(n²)       O(n²)        O(n²)       O(1)
Insertion Sort  O(n)        O(n²)        O(n²)       O(1)
Merge Sort      O(n log n)  O(n log n)   O(n log n)  O(n)
Quick Sort      O(n log n)  O(n log n)   O(n²)       O(log n)*
Heap Sort       O(n log n)  O(n log n)   O(n log n)  O(1)
```

The exact space usage of Quick Sort depends on the implementation and recursion depth. The table represents a typical recursive implementation with reasonably balanced partitions.

sections.title: Java Built-In Sorting
Sorting Custom Objects
Common Sorting Mistakes
sections.content:
A common mistake is choosing a sorting algorithm without considering the input size and characteristics.

Using Bubble Sort on a very large dataset can be unnecessarily expensive, while Counting Sort can consume excessive memory if the value range is huge.

Another mistake is assuming that every O(n log n) sorting algorithm behaves identically. Stability, memory usage, worst-case behavior, cache performance, and input distribution can all matter.

When sorting objects, developers should also be careful about comparator logic and integer overflow when subtracting values to compare them. Prefer explicit comparison methods such as Integer.compare when appropriate.

sections.title: How to Choose a Sorting Algorithm
sections.content:
The right sorting algorithm depends on the problem requirements.

For small or nearly sorted data, Insertion Sort can be useful because of its simplicity and adaptive behavior.

When guaranteed O(n log n) time is important, Merge Sort or Heap Sort can be considered depending on memory and stability requirements.

Quick Sort is widely used because of its strong average performance and good practical behavior, but its worst-case behavior depends on pivot selection and implementation.

Counting Sort and Radix Sort can outperform comparison-based algorithms when the input has suitable integer or digit characteristics.

In production Java applications, standard library sorting methods are usually preferred unless there is a specific reason to implement a custom algorithm.

sections.title: Why Sorting Matters
sections.content:
Sorting is a foundational algorithmic technique. It appears directly in many interview problems and indirectly inside many other algorithms and data structures.

Understanding sorting teaches important concepts such as comparison, divide and conquer, partitioning, recursion, stability, auxiliary memory, and time complexity.

More importantly, recognizing when data should be sorted can simplify an otherwise complicated problem. Many problems that seem difficult become easier after arranging the input in a useful order.

topics.title: Numeric Algorithms
topics.description: Learn fundamental numeric algorithms used to solve mathematical and number-based programming problems, including divisibility, prime numbers, GCD, LCM, exponentiation, digit manipulation, number reversal, Fibonacci numbers, and common mathematical patterns.

sections.title: What Are Numeric Algorithms?
sections.content:
Numeric algorithms are algorithms designed to solve problems involving numbers and mathematical operations. They are commonly used for calculations, number properties, divisibility, digit manipulation, sequences, and mathematical optimization.

Examples include finding whether a number is prime, calculating the greatest common divisor, finding the least common multiple, reversing the digits of a number, calculating powers efficiently, and generating Fibonacci numbers.

Numeric algorithms are important because many programming problems can be reduced to a small set of mathematical observations and efficient operations.

sections.title: Checking Even and Odd Numbers
sections.content:
A number is even when it is completely divisible by 2. Otherwise, it is odd.

The remainder operator can determine this directly:

```java
boolean isEven(int number) {
    return number % 2 == 0;
}
```

For example:

```text
10 % 2 = 0  → even
15 % 2 = 1  → odd
```

This is one of the simplest numeric checks and appears frequently inside loops and conditional algorithms.

sections.title: Divisibility
sections.content:
A number a is divisible by b when dividing a by b leaves a remainder of zero.

For example:

```text
20 % 5 = 0
```

so 20 is divisible by 5.

In Java:

```java
boolean isDivisible(int number, int divisor) {
    return divisor != 0 && number % divisor == 0;
}
```

Divisibility checks are useful in prime testing, factorization, mathematical simulations, and many coding-interview problems.

sections.title: Factors of a Number
Prime Numbers
sections.content:
A prime number is a positive integer greater than 1 that has exactly two positive divisors: 1 and itself.

Examples include:

```text
2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17
```

Numbers such as 1, 4, 6, and 9 are not prime because they have additional divisors.

The number 2 is the only even prime number. Every other even number greater than 2 is composite.

sections.title: Checking Whether a Number Is Prime
Generating Prime Numbers with the Sieve of Eratosthenes
sections.content:
When we need all prime numbers up to a limit n, checking every number independently can be inefficient. The Sieve of Eratosthenes solves this by marking composite numbers systematically.

The process starts by assuming numbers from 2 through n are prime. For each prime p, multiples of p are marked as composite.

For example, when processing 2, values such as 4, 6, 8, and 10 are marked. Then 3 marks 6, 9, 12, and so on.

Only prime numbers remain unmarked.

The sieve runs in approximately O(n log log n) time and requires O(n) space.

sections.title: Sieve of Eratosthenes in Java
Greatest Common Divisor
sections.content:
The Greatest Common Divisor (GCD), also called the Greatest Common Factor, is the largest positive integer that divides two numbers without a remainder.

For example:

```text
GCD(48, 18) = 6
```

because 6 is the largest number that divides both 48 and 18.

The Euclidean algorithm provides an efficient way to calculate GCD using the relationship:

```text
GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a % b)
```

The process continues until the second value becomes zero.

sections.title: Euclidean Algorithm for GCD
Least Common Multiple
sections.content:
The Least Common Multiple (LCM) is the smallest positive integer that is divisible by both numbers.

For example:

```text
LCM(4, 6) = 12
```

For non-zero integers, LCM can be calculated using GCD:

```text
LCM(a, b) = |a / GCD(a, b) × b|
```

Dividing before multiplying can reduce the risk of intermediate overflow compared with directly calculating a × b first.

sections.title: LCM in Java
Power of a Number
sections.content:
Exponentiation calculates a number raised to a power.

For example:

```text
2^5 = 32
```

A straightforward approach multiplies the base by itself exponent times, which takes O(n) multiplications.

A faster technique called exponentiation by squaring reduces the number of multiplications to O(log n).

sections.title: Fast Exponentiation
Counting Digits
Sum of Digits
Reversing a Number
Palindrome Number
Armstrong Number
sections.content:
An Armstrong number is a number that equals the sum of its digits raised to the power of the number of digits.

For example, 153 has three digits:

```text
1³ + 5³ + 3³
= 1 + 125 + 27
= 153
```

Therefore, 153 is an Armstrong number.

The algorithm first counts the digits and then calculates the required power for each digit.

sections.title: Fibonacci Sequence
sections.content:
The Fibonacci sequence is a sequence in which each value is the sum of the previous two values.

A common definition starts with 0 and 1:

```text
0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ...
```

The recurrence is:

```text
F(n) = F(n - 1) + F(n - 2)
```

A simple recursive implementation directly follows the definition but has exponential time complexity because it repeatedly calculates the same values.

sections.title: Efficient Fibonacci Calculation
Checking Powers of Two
sections.content:
A positive integer is a power of two if it can be represented as 2^k for some non-negative integer k.

For example:

```text
1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64
```

For a positive integer, a useful bitwise property is:

```text
n & (n - 1) == 0
```

when n is a power of two.

Java implementation:

```java
boolean isPowerOfTwo(int n) {
    return n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;
}
```

This works because powers of two have exactly one set bit in their binary representation.

sections.title: Checking Perfect Numbers
sections.content:
A perfect number is a positive integer equal to the sum of its positive proper divisors, excluding the number itself.

For example:

```text
6 → divisors: 1, 2, 3
1 + 2 + 3 = 6
```

Therefore, 6 is a perfect number.

Another well-known example is 28:

```text
1 + 2 + 4 + 7 + 14 = 28
```

Factor-pair techniques can reduce the number of divisor checks from O(n) to O(sqrt(n)).

sections.title: Modular Arithmetic
sections.content:
The modulo operator gives the remainder after integer division and is fundamental to many numeric algorithms.

For example:

```text
17 % 5 = 2
```

Modulo arithmetic is useful for checking divisibility, extracting digits, working with cyclic values, calculating results under a modulus, and preventing numbers from growing too large in certain algorithms.

For example, a cyclic index can be calculated as:

```java
int next = (index + 1) % size;
```

This returns to zero when the index reaches the end.

sections.title: Integer Overflow
Mathematical Optimization in Numeric Algorithms
sections.content:
Many numeric problems can be made significantly faster by recognizing mathematical patterns.

For example, checking whether a number is prime does not require testing every value from 2 to n. Testing divisors only up to sqrt(n) is sufficient.

Similarly, exponentiation does not require multiplying the base n times. Exponentiation by squaring reduces the number of operations to O(log n).

These optimizations are important because numeric algorithms often start with a simple brute-force solution and then become efficient through mathematical reasoning.

sections.title: Common Numeric Algorithm Mistakes
sections.content:
A common mistake is ignoring edge cases such as zero, one, negative numbers, and empty or invalid ranges.

For example, 1 is not a prime number, division by zero is invalid, and reversing an integer can overflow its data type.

Another common mistake is using O(n) approaches when a mathematical property allows O(sqrt(n)) or O(log n) behavior.

Developers should also be careful with integer division, negative modulo behavior, and intermediate overflow.

Before implementing a numeric algorithm, identify the input constraints and determine whether the chosen numeric type can safely represent every intermediate value.

sections.title: Numeric Algorithm Complexity
sections.content:
The complexity of numeric algorithms depends on the mathematical operation and the size of the input.

Common examples include:

```text
Check even/odd       O(1)
GCD                  O(log n)
Prime check          O(sqrt(n))
Count digits         O(log n)
Reverse digits       O(log n)
Digit sum            O(log n)
Fast exponentiation  O(log n)
Sieve of Eratosthenes O(n log log n)
```

Here, log n often represents the number of digits or the number of times a value can be repeatedly divided by a constant factor.

Understanding these bounds helps determine whether an algorithm will scale for the expected input size.

sections.title: Why Numeric Algorithms Matter
sections.content:
Numeric algorithms form the foundation of many programming and computer-science problems. They teach how mathematical properties can replace unnecessary brute-force computation.

Prime checking, GCD, LCM, exponentiation, digit manipulation, Fibonacci sequences, modular arithmetic, and number-property checks appear frequently in coding interviews and competitive programming.

The most important skill is not memorizing every algorithm. It is learning to identify mathematical patterns, understand the constraints, handle edge cases, and choose an implementation with appropriate time and space complexity.

topics.title: SEARCHING
topics.description: Learn how searching algorithms locate elements in collections, including Linear Search, Binary Search, Jump Search, Interpolation Search, and search techniques for arrays, strings, and sorted data.

sections.title: What Is Searching?
sections.content:
Searching is the process of finding a particular element or determining whether an element exists in a collection of data.

For example, given:

```text
[10, 25, 30, 45, 60]
```

we may want to determine whether 45 exists and, if it does, find its position.

Searching is one of the most common operations in programming. The appropriate searching technique depends on factors such as whether the data is sorted, how large the collection is, and whether the data changes frequently.

sections.title: Why Searching Matters
sections.content:
Efficient searching is important because applications frequently need to locate records, users, files, products, transactions, or other data.

A simple approach may inspect every element, but this can become expensive as the dataset grows.

For example, searching an unsorted array of one million elements may require checking many elements. If the data is sorted, Binary Search can repeatedly eliminate half of the remaining search space.

The key skill is recognizing what information about the data can be used to reduce unnecessary work.

sections.title: Linear Search
sections.content:
Linear Search is the simplest searching algorithm. It checks elements one by one from the beginning until the target is found or the collection is exhausted.

For example, searching for 30:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
        ↑
      target
```

The algorithm checks 10, then 20, and finally finds 30.

Linear Search does not require the data to be sorted, which makes it useful for unsorted collections.

sections.title: Linear Search in Java
Linear Search Complexity
sections.content:
If the target is the first element, Linear Search takes O(1) time.

If the target is near the end or does not exist, the algorithm may inspect every element, resulting in O(n) time.

Therefore:

```text
Best case:   O(1)
Average:     O(n)
Worst case:  O(n)
Space:       O(1)
```

Linear Search is often appropriate when the collection is small, unsorted, or searched only occasionally.

sections.title: Binary Search
sections.content:
Binary Search is an efficient searching algorithm for sorted data. It repeatedly compares the target with the middle element and eliminates half of the remaining search space.

Consider:

```text
[10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70]
```

To search for 60, start with the middle value 40. Since 60 is greater than 40, everything to the left of 40 can be ignored.

The search continues in the right half until the target is found or no elements remain.

sections.title: Binary Search Process
sections.content:
Binary Search maintains three positions:

- low: beginning of the current search range
- high: end of the current search range
- mid: middle position of the range

The basic process is:

```text
1. Calculate the middle index.
2. Compare arr[mid] with the target.
3. If equal, return mid.
4. If target is smaller, search the left half.
5. If target is larger, search the right half.
6. Repeat until low > high.
```

Each iteration removes approximately half of the remaining candidates.

sections.title: Binary Search in Java
Binary Search Complexity
sections.content:
Binary Search eliminates approximately half of the remaining search space on every iteration.

Therefore, the time complexity is:

```text
Best case:   O(1)
Average:     O(log n)
Worst case:  O(log n)
```

An iterative implementation uses O(1) extra space.

A recursive implementation uses O(log n) call-stack space in the worst case.

The major requirement is that the data must be sorted according to the ordering used by the search.

sections.title: Finding the First Occurrence
Finding the Last Occurrence
Lower Bound
sections.content:
A lower bound is the first position where a value greater than or equal to the target can be placed while maintaining sorted order.

For example:

```text
[10, 20, 20, 30, 40]
```

The lower bound of 20 is index 1.

The lower bound of 25 is index 3 because 30 is the first value greater than or equal to 25.

This concept is widely used in Binary Search problems involving insertion positions, ranges, and duplicate values.

sections.title: Upper Bound
sections.content:
An upper bound is the first position where a value strictly greater than the target occurs.

For:

```text
[10, 20, 20, 30, 40]
```

the upper bound of 20 is index 3 because 30 is the first value greater than 20.

The difference between upper bound and lower bound can be used to determine how many times a value occurs in a sorted array.

sections.title: Counting Occurrences Using Binary Search
sections.content:
In a sorted array, the number of occurrences of a target can be calculated using its first and last positions.

Alternatively, using lower and upper bounds:

```text
count = upperBound(target) - lowerBound(target)
```

For example:

```text
[10, 20, 20, 20, 30]
```

For target 20:

```text
lowerBound = 1
upperBound = 4
count = 4 - 1 = 3
```

This approach takes O(log n) time instead of scanning all elements.

sections.title: Searching in a Binary Search Tree
sections.content:
A Binary Search Tree also supports efficient searching because its values follow an ordering rule.

At each node:

- If the target equals the node value, it is found.
- If the target is smaller, move to the left subtree.
- If the target is larger, move to the right subtree.

For a balanced BST, search takes O(log n) time. For a highly skewed ordinary BST, it can degrade to O(n).

Self-balancing trees such as AVL trees maintain O(log n) worst-case search complexity.

sections.title: Jump Search
sections.content:
Jump Search is designed for sorted arrays. Instead of checking every element, it jumps ahead by fixed-size blocks and then performs a linear search within the block where the target may exist.

A commonly used jump size is approximately sqrt(n).

For example, for an array of 16 elements, a jump size of about 4 can be used.

The algorithm first jumps through positions 0, 4, 8, 12, and so on. Once the target range is identified, it performs a linear scan within that block.

Its typical time complexity is O(sqrt(n)).

sections.title: Jump Search in Java
Interpolation Search
sections.content:
Interpolation Search is another search technique for sorted data. Instead of always examining the middle element like Binary Search, it estimates where the target is likely to be based on the values at the boundaries.

It works particularly well when values are approximately uniformly distributed.

For example, if searching for a value close to the maximum in a uniformly distributed range, Interpolation Search may jump closer to the end rather than always starting from the middle.

Its average complexity can approach O(log log n) for suitable uniformly distributed data, but its worst-case complexity is O(n).

sections.title: Exponential Search
sections.content:
Exponential Search is useful when the size of the sorted search space is unknown or potentially very large.

The algorithm first checks positions that grow exponentially:

```text
1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, ...
```

Once it finds a range that may contain the target, it performs Binary Search within that range.

The typical complexity is O(log n) for a sorted array, while the technique is particularly useful when the target is located relatively close to the beginning or when the search boundary is not known in advance.

sections.title: Searching in a Rotated Sorted Array
sections.content:
A rotated sorted array was originally sorted but then shifted around a pivot.

For example:

```text
Original: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]
Rotated:  [40, 50, 60, 10, 20, 30]
```

A modified Binary Search can still work in O(log n) time when values are distinct.

At every step, at least one of the two halves is guaranteed to be sorted. The algorithm determines which half is sorted and checks whether the target falls inside that range.

sections.title: Binary Search on the Answer
sections.content:
Binary Search is not limited to finding a value inside an array. It can also be applied to a numeric answer when the problem has a monotonic condition.

Suppose we need to find the minimum capacity that can satisfy a requirement. If capacity X works, every capacity greater than X also works.

The possible answers therefore have a pattern like:

```text
false false false true true true
```

Binary Search can locate the first true value efficiently.

This technique is commonly called Binary Search on the Answer and appears in scheduling, allocation, capacity, partitioning, and optimization problems.

sections.title: Searching Strings
Hash-Based Searching
Choosing a Searching Algorithm
sections.content:
The choice of searching technique depends on the structure of the data.

For an unsorted small collection, Linear Search is simple and often sufficient.

For a sorted array, Binary Search is usually the natural choice because it provides O(log n) searching.

For repeated membership checks without requiring sorted order, a hash-based structure such as HashSet may be more appropriate.

For sorted data with special characteristics, Jump Search or Interpolation Search may be considered. For unknown search boundaries, Exponential Search can be useful.

The key is to identify what properties of the data can be exploited before choosing an algorithm.

sections.title: Common Searching Mistakes
sections.content:
A common mistake is applying Binary Search to unsorted data. Binary Search depends on the ordering of the search space, so using it on arbitrary unsorted values produces incorrect results.

Another mistake is using the wrong boundary updates. When arr[mid] is smaller than the target, the new range must move to mid + 1. When arr[mid] is larger, the range must move to mid - 1.

Developers also frequently introduce off-by-one errors when implementing first occurrence, last occurrence, lower bound, and upper bound searches.

For Binary Search, carefully defining whether the search range is inclusive or exclusive helps avoid these errors.

sections.title: Searching Complexity Comparison
sections.content:
Different searching techniques have different requirements and performance characteristics.

```text
Algorithm              Best       Average       Worst        Requirement
Linear Search          O(1)       O(n)          O(n)         None
Binary Search          O(1)       O(log n)      O(log n)     Sorted data
Jump Search             O(1)       O(sqrt n)     O(sqrt n)    Sorted data
Interpolation Search    O(1)       O(log log n)* O(n)         Sorted, suitable distribution
Hash Lookup             O(1)       O(1)*         O(n)*        Hash structure
```

The values marked with * depend on assumptions such as distribution, hashing behavior, and implementation details.

In practice, data structure choice can be as important as the search algorithm itself.

sections.title: Why Searching Matters
sections.content:
Searching is a fundamental algorithmic operation because almost every useful application needs to locate or verify data.

The most important lesson is that search performance depends heavily on how the data is organized. An unsorted array may require a linear scan, while sorted data enables Binary Search and hash-based structures can provide fast average membership checks without sorting.

Understanding Linear Search, Binary Search, search boundaries, rotated-array search, and Binary Search on the Answer provides a strong foundation for many array, tree, graph, and interview problems.

topics.title: STRINGS
topics.description: Learn how strings are represented, manipulated, searched, compared, and processed in data-structure and algorithm problems. This topic covers string traversal, common operations, character frequencies, transformations, pattern matching basics, and practical techniques used in coding interviews.

sections.title: What Is a String?
sections.content:
A string is a sequence of characters used to represent text. Strings are one of the most common data types in programming and appear in problems involving text processing, searching, validation, parsing, and pattern matching.

For example, the string `"hello"` contains five characters: `h`, `e`, `l`, `l`, and `o`. Each character has a position, or index, starting from zero in most programming languages.

Strings can contain letters, digits, spaces, punctuation, and special characters. In algorithm problems, treating a string as a sequence of characters is often the first step toward solving the problem.

sections.title: Why Strings Matter in DSA
sections.content:
String problems are common in coding interviews because they combine basic data structures with algorithmic thinking. Many problems can be solved by scanning characters, maintaining frequency counts, using two pointers, or applying hashing.

Typical string problems include:

- Checking whether a string is a palindrome.
- Counting character frequencies.
- Finding duplicate characters.
- Removing or replacing characters.
- Checking whether two strings are anagrams.
- Finding substrings and subsequences.
- Searching for patterns.
- Validating formatted input.

A strong understanding of strings also makes problems involving arrays, hash maps, stacks, queues, and dynamic programming easier to understand.

sections.title: String Indexing
sections.content:
Characters in a string can usually be accessed using their index. The first character has index `0`, the second has index `1`, and so on.

For the string `"HELLO"`:

- `H` is at index 0.
- `E` is at index 1.
- `L` is at index 2.
- `L` is at index 3.
- `O` is at index 4.

The last valid index is `length - 1`.

When iterating through a string, a common pattern is to start at zero and continue while the index is less than the string length.

sections.title: Strings in Java
String Immutability
Traversing a String
Common String Operations
Comparing Strings
String Concatenation
StringBuilder
Character Frequency
Using HashMap for Strings
Palindrome Strings
Two-Pointer String Technique
sections.content:
Two pointers are useful when a string must be processed from both ends or when two positions move through the string at different rates.

For palindrome checking, one pointer starts at the beginning and another at the end. After comparing the characters, the pointers move toward the center.

The technique avoids creating a reversed copy of the string and can therefore reduce additional memory usage.

Two pointers are also useful for problems involving removing characters, comparing ranges, validating sequences, and processing strings with special rules.

sections.title: Anagrams
Substrings
Subsequence
String Reversal
Removing Duplicate Characters
Case Conversion
Pattern Searching Basics
sections.content:
Pattern searching means finding occurrences of one string inside another string. Given a text and a pattern, the goal may be to determine whether the pattern exists, find its first occurrence, or find every occurrence.

A simple brute-force approach checks the pattern at every possible starting position.

If the text has length n and the pattern has length m, the worst-case complexity of naive matching can be O(n × m).

More advanced algorithms such as KMP, Rabin-Karp, and Z-algorithm improve performance for specific types of pattern-searching problems.

sections.title: Naive String Matching
Sliding Window on Strings
sections.content:
The sliding-window technique is particularly useful for substring problems. Instead of repeatedly examining every possible substring, maintain a window with a left and right boundary and update it as the right boundary moves.

Typical problems include:

- Longest substring without repeating characters.
- Minimum window containing required characters.
- Longest substring with at most K distinct characters.
- Finding anagrams inside a larger string.

A sliding window often reduces a quadratic brute-force solution to O(n) or O(n log n), depending on the data structure used to maintain the window.

sections.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
String Sorting
sections.content:
Strings can be sorted lexicographically, which means they are ordered according to character comparison rules.

For example, Java can sort an array of strings using:

```java
String[] words = {"banana", "apple", "orange"};
Arrays.sort(words);
```

Sorting is useful when solving anagram-related problems or when the problem requires ordered output.

For an anagram check, sorting both strings gives a simple solution with O(n log n) time. Frequency counting can reduce this to O(n) when the character set is known and limited.

sections.title: Common String Mistakes
sections.content:
Several mistakes appear repeatedly in string-based coding problems:

- Using `==` instead of `equals()` for Java string content comparison.
- Forgetting that indexes start at zero.
- Accessing `charAt(length)` instead of `charAt(length - 1)`.
- Confusing a substring with a subsequence.
- Creating many temporary strings inside a large loop.
- Forgetting to handle an empty string.
- Assuming all characters are lowercase English letters when the problem allows other characters.
- Ignoring spaces, punctuation, or case when the problem requires normalization.
- Using a quadratic solution when a frequency map or sliding window can solve the problem more efficiently.

sections.title: String Complexity Considerations
sections.content:
The complexity of a string algorithm depends on both the string length and the operations performed on it.

A single traversal is usually O(n). Comparing two strings of length n can require O(n) time. Sorting characters generally takes O(n log n). Naive pattern matching can take O(n × m), where n is the text length and m is the pattern length.

When analyzing a solution, look beyond the main loop. Repeated calls to operations that create or copy strings can introduce additional costs.

For interview problems, clearly identify the input size, the number of scans, and any auxiliary data structures used.

sections.title: Choosing the Right String Technique
sections.content:
Different string problems call for different techniques.

Use direct traversal when each character only needs to be processed once. Use a frequency array when the alphabet is small and fixed. Use a hash map when the character set is dynamic. Use two pointers when processing characters from both ends. Use a sliding window for substring constraints that change as the window moves. Use sorting when character order does not matter and an O(n log n) solution is acceptable.

The key skill is recognizing the structure of the problem rather than memorizing one string algorithm.

sections.title: Why Strings Matter in DSA
sections.content:
Strings provide a practical way to learn several core algorithmic patterns: traversal, hashing, two pointers, sliding windows, sorting, and pattern matching. These techniques appear far beyond text processing and are frequently reused in array and sequence problems.

Before solving a string problem, identify whether the problem is about individual characters, character frequencies, contiguous substrings, subsequences, ordering, or pattern occurrence. That classification often points directly toward the appropriate data structure or algorithm.

A strong command of string manipulation is therefore an important part of interview preparation and general problem-solving.
